strengths: Important domain-specific contribution: Addresses a clear gap in video foundation models, which are predominantly human-centric and struggle to generalize to fine-grained non-human primate behavior analysis.

Well-structured curation pipeline: Combines 174 hours of observational research footage across 11 field/captive sites with 250 hours of web-sourced videos, utilizing shot detection, a CLIP-based relevance classifier, and zero-shot detection filtering to curate a high-quality 424-hour dataset (PriVi).

Effective and parameter-efficient readout design: The proposed attentive probe applies a severe bottleneck downprojection (from 1024 to 64 dimensions) alongside per-class learned query tokens, effectively mitigating overfitting on small animal behavior datasets with only 220k parameters.

Strong and consistent empirical performance: Pretraining V-JEPA on PriVi yields substantial gains across four distinct primate behavior benchmarks (PanAf500, ChimpACT, BaboonLand, and ChimpBehave), consistently surpassing strong baselines such as VideoMAEv2, ChimpVLM, and standard V-JEPA.

Thorough ablation studies: Validates the necessity of automated relevance filtering (comparing to YT-Random), primate-centric cropping, continual in-domain pretraining, and the specific design choices of the attentive classifier.
weaknesses: Unsubstantiated low-label scaling claims: The abstract and introduction emphasize that the framework 'scales favorably with fewer labels' and is promising for low-label regimes, but the paper does not include dedicated label-efficiency curves (e.g., evaluating with 1%, 5%, 10%, or 20% labeled downstream data).

Reliance on ground-truth boxes at downstream evaluation: Across the four evaluated benchmarks, behavior classification is performed on crops centered on ground-truth bounding boxes, which bypasses the real-world challenge of automated spatio-temporal animal detection and tracking.
Partial dataset release: 14% of the curated pretraining data is withheld due to ongoing research restrictions, which slightly hampers exact pretraining reproducibility.

Modest algorithmic novelty: The work is primarily data-centric, combining existing off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO, CLIP, V-JEPA, standard attention layers) rather than proposing new foundational learning objectives or architectural paradigms.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in wildlife computer vision: the scarcity of domain-specific video data and the domain gap present in standard human-centric foundation models when analyzing wild animal behavior.

Presents a well-motivated and scalable data curation pipeline combining scene cut detection, CLIP-based relevance filtering, and zero-shot open-set detection (Grounding DINO) to handle the noise and empty frames typical of in-the-wild and web-sourced footage.

Comprehensive empirical validation across four diverse primate behavior benchmarks (PanAf500, ChimpACT, BaboonLand, and ChimpBehave), consistently demonstrating improvements over strong prior models such as VideoPrism, VideoMAEv2, and ChimpVLM.

Thoughtful design of the frozen attentive evaluation head: aggressively downprojecting latent representations to prevent overfitting on small-scale animal behavior datasets while preserving depth, supported by insightful ablation studies.
weaknesses: The abstract and introduction emphasize that the proposed approach 'scales favorably with fewer labels' and is promising for low-label regimes, but the experimental section lacks explicit label-efficiency experiments (e.g., varying labeled fractions like 1%, 5%, 10%, or few-shot evaluations).

Evaluation depends on ground-truth primate bounding box crops during downstream testing, which limits evaluation to pre-localized action classification rather than full end-to-end spatiotemporal behavior detection on uncurated video footage.
Pretraining reproducibility is somewhat hindered by the fact that 14% of the curated dataset consists of unreleased camera trap footage from ongoing studies that cannot be made publicly available.

strengths: Addresses an impactful and challenging domain (computational ethology and conservation) where human-centric video foundation models typically demonstrate suboptimal transfer.

Presents a well-motivated and automated data curation pipeline combining shot boundary detection, zero-shot detection (Grounding DINO), and CLIP-based relevance filtering to clean and balance heterogeneous video sources.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four distinct primate behavior benchmarks (PanAf500, ChimpACT, BaboonLand, and ChimpBehave), achieving consistent and noticeable improvements over both human-centric foundation models and dataset-specific baselines.

The proposed narrow attentive classifier head is simple, parameter-efficient (220k parameters), and effectively mitigates overfitting when evaluating frozen backbones on small-scale behavior datasets.
Clear ablation studies that systematically validate the contributions of the data filtering stages, primate-centric cropping, and classifier architecture choices.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is relatively limited, as the methodology primarily integrates existing components (V-JEPA pretraining, Grounding DINO, CLIP, PySceneDetect) without introducing fundamentally new pretraining objectives.
All downstream evaluations rely on ground-truth bounding box crops rather than evaluating end-to-end detection and spatio-temporal action recognition in full uncropped scenes.
Reproducibility of the pretraining data is partially constrained, as 14% of the R&O corpus cannot be publicly released due to privacy/ongoing research agreements.
While PriVi covers multiple primate families (e.g., lemurs, marmosets), downstream evaluation is limited exclusively to chimpanzees and baboons due to the scarcity of annotated public benchmarks.
